newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar closes mid-range after see-saw day.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar closes mid-range after see-saw day.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar closed well-supported and around the middle of its range on Wednesday after a see-saw ride driven by domestic political news, an Australian rate cut and the U.S. presidential election.
A NZ$100 million three year bond issue by Walt Disney Co lent the currency a very firm tone overnight, carrying it to a high of US$0.7118.
It gapped lower in the morning after caretaker Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith, who is also deputy finance minister, said it was higher than the strength of the economy suggested.

The Kiwi was closing at 0.7096/03 and 67.81 on its Trade-Weighted Index, around the middle of its 0.7087-7115 range. "It's closing mid-level, but with a reasonably bid tone," one senior foreign exchange manager said.

Dealers said U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election and the Republicans' Senate victory were seen as good for the U.S. dollar. There had been suggestions that a sweeping Democrat win in both houses could delay U.S. attempts to balance the budget.
"That's been dollar supportive, with dollar/yen being up near its highs, so that's supporting our TWI as well," the forex manager said.

There were rumours of another NZ$150 million dual currency samurai issue, with the prospect of yet more to come this week and next. The dealer saw kiwi testing its highs again overnight, with a range of 0.7095-7125/30.

Another dealer said there was good foreign demand around the 0.7080-90 level, with buying seen out of Japan during the session. He also saw the U.S. election outcome lending support to the TWI and increasing appetite for kiwi/yen.
The Kiwi was also supported by the Australian dollar, despite the central bank's half point cut in official cash rates to 6.5 percent.

"The Aussies cut their rates, as was pretty well expected, and that was a classic case of 'sell the rumour, buy the fact', with the Aussie immediately going up...The market was essentially short going into it and has basically squared itself up," he said.
